evidence_concerns.message: Table 1 prints Kraken relative abundances of 5.17E‐10 (Salmonella enterica and Escherichia coli), 5.17E‐11 (Lactobacillus fermentum) and 5.17E‐12 (Enterococcus faecalis): one mantissa over three orders of magnitude. As read fractions these need at least about 2 billion to 190 billion reads per assigned read, far above the study's libraries (patient samples average 33.5 M reads after QC; the control library size is not given). The values are probably a computation or formatting artefact, so the Kraken column of Table 1 and its eta squared (3.20E‐2) should not be compared. Values are kept as printed. Table 2 values are not affected by this finding.

evidence_concerns.message: The column labelled 'NTv3' in Figure 1b and 1c is not the method the Methods describe. The manuscript repository's plotting code (scripts/figure1/_heatmap_common.py at e5e4a43) renames 'NTv3 cosine dist' to 'NTv3' and drops 'NTv3 subref probe', whereas Methods 'Baseline methods' describe NTv3 650M layer-11 embeddings with L2-regularised logistic regression under 5-fold gene-holdout cross-validation. limitations: Preprint, not peer reviewed. No published version was found (bioRxiv publication API, 2026-10-13).
Results are printed only as aggregates: Table 2 over all 24 tasks and Table 4 per domain. Per-task leaderboard percentiles appear only as points in Figures 2 and 4, with no printed values.

Table 3 names two protein engineering tasks differently from the repository's task list at commit 673f3d8 (experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt): SPA_STAAU_Tsuboyama_2023 (protein A) versus SBI_STAAM_Tsuboyama_2023_2JVG (immunoglobulin-binding protein Sbi, single substitutions), and PSAE_PICP2_indels versus PSAE_PICP2_Tsuboyama_2023_1PSE (the substitution assay; the repository also holds a separate _indels task). Which of these assays were run is unresolved. The third label difference, CBX4_HUMAN_multi-sub versus CBX4_HUMAN_Tsuboyama_2023_2K28, is the same assay: the repository description of 2K28 says it contains multi-substitution variants of CBX4_HUMAN.

Table 4 prints a value with a plus-or-minus spread but its caption does not say what the spread is. Figures 2 and 4 show the same per-domain leaderboard percentiles as mean ± SEM across tasks, and the Table 2 caption refers to the reported SEM.

Section 3.4 defines Above Median, Any Medal and Completion Rate over tasks, but the Table 4 values are multiples of 1/(4 x tasks in the domain) (for example 45.8% = 11/24 for 6 protein tasks), which fits counting replicate runs. The denominator is unresolved.
Table 4 prints Completion Rate 'NA' for Dummy in the penalized block, while Table 2 prints 100.0 for Dummy overall.
All agents were run by the benchmark's authors, who did not build them. B. T. is CTO of ScienceMachine, which provided compute and LLM API resources (Competing Interests; Acknowledgments).

Version 3 replaced the STELLA rows for Drug Discovery and Protein Engineering in Table 4 (and STELLA's Table 2 rows) with new values without explaining why in the text; for example STELLA's penalized protein engineering leaderboard percentile is 14.78 in v2 and 34.98 in v3, and its completion rate 87.5 and 100.0. The other agents' rows are unchanged, including their Mean Rank, which leaves the Mean Rank columns of those blocks internally inconsistent (they no longer sum to 15). Those 20 Mean Rank results are marked disputed.

Section 4.2 says Biomni leads Protein Engineering with penalties applied; that sentence is unchanged from v2. In v3 Table 4 STELLA has the higher penalized protein engineering leaderboard percentile (34.98 vs 29.93) and Above Median (45.8 vs 25.0); Biomni has the better Mean Rank (2.00 vs 2.33).
M. G. is a contract employee of ScienceMachine, as well as B. T. being its CTO (Competing Interests).

limitations: The repository holds no agent results or leaderboard snapshots; the human leaderboards are fetched from upstream services at grading time.

Agent configuration files are the repository defaults at this commit. The paper does not say the reported runs used exactly these files, and some differ from Section 3 (STELLA's model, per-agent time limits).

Time limits: the runner overrides each agent's TIME_LIMIT_SECS with the task's time_limit when one is set (biomlbench/agents.py, agents/registry.py). 18 of the 20 in-scope tasks set 28800 s (8 hours), matching Section 3.4. Q8EG35_SHEON_Campbell_2022_indels and CSN4_MOUSE_Tsuboyama_2023_1UFM_indels set none, so the agent default would apply (43200 s for AIDE, Biomni and MLAgentBench; 57600 s for STELLA).

Reference leaderboards are not all human submissions: for ProteinGym tasks the leaderboard is the row of ProteinGym's own leaderboard for that assay, one entry per published model (biomlbench/data_sources/proteingym.py, with a placeholder submission date), and the Open Problems spatially-variable-genes description says its leaderboard 'is comprised of existing methods'. The manual (Open Problems) data source returns an empty leaderboard at this commit, so how the single-cell leaderboards were built is not recoverable from the repository.

All six ProteinGym task configs set awards_medals: false, yet Table 4 prints non-zero Any Medal values for protein engineering; the grader computes medal thresholds from leaderboard size regardless of that flag (biomlbench/grade_helpers.py).

evidence_concerns.message: Appendix A.2 describes the random baseline as predicting hit with probability equal to 'the overall proportion of actual hits in the specific benchmark dataset'. With one pooled rate (485 of 1,175 = 41.3%, Table 3) the expected PPV, sensitivity, F1 and FPR are all about 0.41 and specificity and NPV about 0.59. Table 8 prints PPV 0.47, sensitivity 0.46, F1 0.47, FPR 0.36, specificity 0.64 and NPV 0.63. With each screen's own hit rate (Table 3) the expected values are 0.47, 0.47, 0.47, 0.37, 0.63 and 0.63, which match. One draw at the pooled rate would need sensitivity about 2 standard errors above and FPR about 3 below expectation at once. The baseline therefore probably uses per-screen hit rates, which is information a screen designer would not have before the screen. The expected values were computed by the reviewer from Table 3 counts and are not stored as results. Treat the random row as a per-screen-prevalence classifier, not a matched random-selection comparator.
evidence_concerns.source_locator: Appendix A.2; Table 3; Table 1, row "Random Baseline"; Table 8, row "Random N/A N/A"

attributes.version: bioRxiv preprint version 1, posted 2026-10-09; full-text PDF (11 pages)
limitations: Preprint, not peer reviewed; single author (712 North Inc.), no funding; none of the evaluated models was developed by the author.
The bioRxiv JATS XML holds metadata only, so the tables were read from the PDF text layer.
Supplementary Tables I to VI and the Zenodo material (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23105803) were not retrieved.
Table IV prints 15 (13.9%) for AlphaGenome splice scorer and 31 (28.7%) for Genos 10B ClinVar type I errors; 15/107 is 14.0% and 31/107 is 29.0%.
Not archived in the batch: CC BY-NC-ND licence; hash and locators only.

Four printed accuracies differ from those computed from the same row's counts: Table III Borzoi (128-bp) 89.1% (counts give 89.8%); Table IV AlphaGenome (either module) 71.6% (70.5%), Borzoi (128-bp) 80.9% (81.4%) and Genos 10B 61.7% (61.2%).
attributes.hash_scope: SHA-256 of one retrieval of the bioRxiv PDF. bioRxiv stamps the PDF when serving it (ModDate and the second document ID), so later retrievals differ. A reviewer retrieval on 2026-10-12 of the same length (1,823,372 bytes) had SHA-256 e22491e217c7c158528668b38bcb8b9855b89617b807c60b740795a204c84b0a and ModDate D:20261011221204-07'00'. All 168 Table III and IV cells in that copy match the stored results.

evidence_concerns.message: The AlphaGenome rows of Tables III, IV and the extended OPA1 positive calls come from scripts that pass a 0-based position to AlphaGenome's 1-based genome.Variant, so each variant was applied one base from its true position. The author labelled the report a bug on 2026-10-20 and said rerunning with the 1-based position substantially improved accuracy. The AlphaGenome results are disputed until the rerun is published; the other models' rows are not affected.

attributes.artifact_format: ZIP archive of three Office Open XML workbooks
limitations: Author-deposited supplementary data, not peer reviewed and not a publication in its own right.

Per-variant model calls only: the archive holds classifications ('pathogenic' or 'n.s.'), not the model scores or the thresholds, so the printed sensitivities and specificities cannot be recomputed from it.
The AlphaGenome columns were produced by the scripts carrying the 1-base coordinate offset reported in upstream issue #2, so those calls share the defect of the printed AlphaGenome results.
CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 forbids redistributing the workbooks, so they are not stored in this repository; the archive SHA-256 and classify-table-vi.py are the record.

attributes.version: medRxiv preprint version 1 supplement DC3 (file 344940_file09.xlsx in the JATS XML)
limitations: Table S9 values are spreadsheet formulas over the TP, FN, TN and FP cells of the same row; the stored results are recorded.
Tables S3 to S5 list 22 true-negative rows (6 muscle, 3 fibroblast, 13 cycloheximide-treated fibroblast); Results and Table S9 use 21 true-negative samples.
Results ('True negative analysis reveals high false positive rates') give an OUTRIDER + GTEx false-positive rate of 83%; Table S9 row 8 (TN 1, FP 4) implies 4 of 5 (80%).
Table S9 gives LeafcutterMD 67 positives (TP 0 + FN 67) while FRASER, run on the same three tissue sets, has 68 (TP 21 + FN 47).
Cell I6 (LeafcutterMD F1) holds a typed 0 rather than the row formula; with precision and recall both 0 the F1 formula would be undefined.

Table S7 true-negative rows do not reproduce Table S9 rows 7 and 8: read as in Tables S3, S4 and S8 ('YES' = no outlier), Table S7 gives OUTRIDER 8 of 9 negative samples without outliers (Table S9: 4) and OUTRIDER + GTEx 1 of 6 (Table S9: 1 of 5). The prose rates (56% and 83%) match Table S9 for OUTRIDER and Table S7 for OUTRIDER + GTEx.

name: Crowdsourced Protein Design: Lessons From the Adaptyv EGFR Binder Competition (Cotet et al., bioRxiv 2025)
description: Primary source retrieved and hashed for the 2026-10-22 de novo binder design extraction (issue #176).

evidence_concerns.message: The paper prints three different round-1 binder rates and two round-2 expression rates. Section 2.4 gives round 1 as '2.5% (5/201)' and round 2 as 'a 95% expression rate (378 of 400 tested)'; Section 4.1 gives expression as improving 'from 73% to 94%'; Section 4.1 gives the binder percentage as rising 'from 3% in the first round to 13%'. All the printed values are recorded with their locators and none is reconciled here.
evidence_concerns.source_locator: Sections 2.4, 4.1 and 4.2

evidence_concerns.message: Section 4.1 says Figure 8 shows 'the total number of validated binders across the 3 binding thresholds' but no section of the paper defines those three thresholds. No hit definition is therefore recorded for the Figure 8 counts, and the binding protocol's success threshold is left unstated with a reason rather than guessed.
evidence_concerns.source_locator: Section 4.1; Figure 8 caption

attributes.hash_scope: SHA-256 of one retrieval of a mutable web page. The hash describes that retrieval, not a stable artifact.
limitations: Preprint, not peer reviewed.
Written by the competition organisers, who ran the assay. The designs are the entrants'.

Design methods are self-declared: Section 4.2 states that entrants were asked 'to write a short summary of their workflow, which we manually curated and categorized into five design choices'. There is no controlled assignment of methods to designs.

Entrants chose how much effort to spend and how many designs to submit, and Adaptyv hand-selected 101 of 201 round-1 and 300 of 400 round-2 designs to increase diversity, so the tested set is not a sample of any method's output.
Figure 8 reports binders 'across the 3 binding thresholds' and the body does not define those thresholds anywhere.
No conventional comparator arm. EGF and cetuximab were positive controls for the assay, not a design method evaluated on a set of candidates.
Per-method and per-category hit rates are printed only in Figures 3, 8 and 9 and the 60 affinities only in Figure 10; the figure values were not read.

evidence_concerns.message: Fig. 1b's caption defines success as binding observed on SPR, but the PD-1 screen was BLI in a bivalent Fc-fusion format and the CLDN1 screen used soluble analogues. The 46.3% average therefore pools targets measured under different endpoints.

limitations: Developer-reported: the BindCraft authors built the pipeline, chose the targets and chose which designs to test.

Fig. 1b prints the per-target numerator and denominator inside graphic boxes. Those boxes are not in the JATS text and were not read from the figure image. Where the Results prose states the counts they are recorded from the prose; where it does not (CrSAS-6, CbAgo) no hit count is recorded.

The assay is not uniform across targets. Fig. 1b's caption defines a successful design as one 'where binding was observed on SPR measurement', but PD-1 was screened by BLI in a bivalent Fc-fusion format and the claudin binders were prescreened against soluble analogues rather than the wild-type target.
Denominators are 6 to 53 designs per target and the tested designs are the top-ranked ones by the authors' own in silico filter, so design and selection are coupled.
No conventional comparator was run. The RFdiffusion comparison in Extended Data Fig. 1c is generation time and in silico success rate, and Extended Data Fig. 7 is reprediction of published designs.

Tables 11, 12 and 14 print one value per cell with no uncertainty. Bootstrap standard errors appear only as error bars in Figure 6, which prints no numbers.

The results of FEP+ are intended to show the maximum attainable accuracy of current (commercial) FEP simulations by manually adjusting the protocol (input preparation, perturbation map, force field) to the system at hand after observing the error with respect to the experiment (appendix D.2.2, 'Baselines'), so the FEP+ arm is not a prospective baseline.

The OpenFE arm's cited source is a blog post (Horton, 2025), which is not a primary source under this repository's rules and was not retrieved.

The column headers read 'target avg.' while appendix D.2.2 'Evaluation metrics' defines every regression metric as computed per assay and averaged across assays weighted by compound count. Assays and targets are not the same unit, and the source does not reconcile the two labels.
The paper's claim of being more than 1,000 times faster than FEP is not backed by a measured FEP+ cost: the FEP+ time cell in Table 12 is printed as '-'.
Per-assay and per-series values behind the target averages are not printed anywhere in the supplement. Figure 12 shows per-assay scatter plots for the validation set only and prints no numbers.
